1
INTRODUCTION
Applicants	ask	this	Court	to	suspend	a	district court	judgment	to	which	
they	are	not	parties.	Both	the	district	court	and	Fifth	Circuit have	refused	emergency	 relief, and	Applicants’ appeal	 from	 the	 denial	 of	intervention	 remains	
pending.	The	district	court	denied	their	motion	to	intervene,	App.	88a–94a,	and	
the	 Fifth	Circuit	denied	 both	 their	motion	 to	 stay	 the	Consent	 Judgment	and	
their	 request	 for	 summary	 reversal	 of	 the	intervention	 order,	App.	 98a–99a.	
The	denial	of	intervention	was	based	on	Applicants’	lack	of	standing,	an	issue	
on	which	 there	is	no	circuit	split	and	which	does	not	warrant	review	by	 this	
Court.
Nor	is	a	stay	“necessary	or	appropriate	in	aid	of”	this	Court’s	prospective	
jurisdiction	under	the	All	Writs	Act,	28	U.S.C. § 1651(a). The	Fifth	Circuit	can	
decide	the	pending	intervention	appeal	without	reinstating	the	2024	Administrative	 Closure	Rule.	 If	Applicants	eventually	 become	 parties,	 they	may	 then	
seek	whatever	relief	is	lawfully	available.	Until	then,	suspending	the	judgment	
would	not	preserve	jurisdiction;	it	would	confer	substantive	relief	that	Applicants	presently	lack	standing	and	party	status	to	seek.	The	All	Writs	Act	does	
not	 enlarge	 this	 Court’s	 jurisdiction	 or	 displace	 the	 requirements	 governing	
stays.	Clinton	v.	Goldsmith,	526	U.S.	529,	534–35	(1999).

2
Applicants	also	fail	each	element	of	the	demanding	stay	standard.	Applicants	cannot	demonstrate	a	 reasonable	probability	 that	 this	Court	will	grant	
certiorari.	The	Fifth	Circuit	has	not	decided	the	intervention	appeal,	much	less	
addressed	Applicants’	attacks	on	the	Consent	Judgment.	Applicants	do	not	ask	
the	Court	to	grant	certiorari	before	judgment,	and	they	make	no	showing	that	
this	 case	 satisfies	 Rule	 11’s	 requirement	 of	 “imperative	 public	 importance”	
warranting	departure	from	normal	appellate	practice.	
The	two	cases	on	which	Applicants	principally	rely	do	not	establish	otherwise.	Arizona	v.	City	&	County	of	San	Francisco,	596	U.S.	763	(2022),	was	dismissed	as	improvidently	granted	after	the	Chief	Justice	explained	that	the	surrounding	questions	formed	a	“mare’s	nest”	impeding	review.	Id. at	766	(Roberts,	C.J.,	concurring).	
In	Arizona	v.	Mayorkas,	143	S.	Ct.	478	(2022),	this Court	granted	certiorari	
(which	the	applicants	expressly	requested) only	to	review	the	denial	of	intervention	based	on	timeliness.	See Emergency	Application	for	Stay at	18–19,	No.
22A544 (“This	 Court	 is	 also	 likely	 to	 reverse	 the	 D.C.	 Circuit’s	 denial	 of	 the	
States’ motion	to	intervene	on	timeliness	grounds.”).	In	that	case,	the	applicants	
argued	 that	 certiorari was	 warranted	 because	 the	 D.C.	 Circuit’s	 decision	
“flout[ed] this	Court’s	decisions	in	United	Airlines	and	Cameron,	and	also spli[t]
with	the	decisions	of	its	sister	circuits.”	Id. at	19.	Nothing	similar	is	true	about

3
the	standing	determination	underlying	the	denial	of	intervention	in	this	case,	
which	does	not	warrant	certiorari.
There	is	no	fair	prospect	of	reversal	in	any	event.	Because	the	actual	parties	waived	appeal,	Applicants	must	independently	establish	Article	III	standing	
to	 pursue	 the	 contemplated	merits	appeal.	Virginia	House	 of	Delegates	v.	Bethune-Hill,	587	U.S.	658,	663–64	(2019);	Diamond	v.	Charles,	476	U.S.	54,	68–71	
(1986).	The	district	court	correctly	held	that	none	can.	The	Cities’	lost-tax	theory	requires	 Applicants	to	overcome	a	chain	of	contingencies	like	the	one	in	
Clapper	v.	Amnesty	Intern.	USA,	568	U.S.	398,	409	(2013):	 an	administratively	
closed	case	must	be	 re-calendared;	 the	alien must	lose	on	 the	merits;	a	 final	
removal	order	must	issue;	the	Department	of	Homeland	Security	must	execute	
it; and the	person	otherwise	must	have	remained	employed	and	paying	a	municipal	income	tax. App.	90a–92a.	No	declaration	identifies	even	one	taxpayer	
for	whom	 that	chain	is	likely.	The	U-visa	 theory	is	more	attenuated	still:	 the	
Consent	 Judgment	does	not	alter	U-visa	eligibility,	municipal	certification,	or	
adjudication by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (“USCIS”), and	
the	Cities	identify	no	 victim	who	has	stopped	cooperating,	no	witness	 facing	
imminent	removal,	and	no	prosecution	impaired	by	the	judgment.	App.	92a.
Centro	 Legal’s	 theory	 fails	 under	 this	 Court’s	 organizational-standing	
precedents.	In FDA	v.	Alliance	for	Hippocratic	Medicine,	this	Court	rejected	the

4
expansive	proposition	that	an	organization	establishes	standing	whenever	government	action	causes	it	to	expend	or	reallocate	resources.	602	U.S.	367,	394–
95	(2024).	The	Court	explained	that its	prior	precedent, Havens	Realty	Corp.	v.	
Coleman,	455	U.S.	363	(1982), involved	something	materially	different:	the	defendant’s	 conduct	 “directly	 affected	 and	 interfered	 with”	 the	 organization’s	
“core	business	activities.” Alliance	for	Hippocratic	Medicine,	602	U.S.	at	395.	The	
defendant	committed	a	tortious	act	directly	against	the	plaintiff	by	“provid[ing]
[its]	black	employees	false	information	about	apartment	availability.”	Id. at	395.
The	Consent	 Judgment	does	not	regulate	Centro	Legal,	deny	it	access	 to	
clients,	or	obstruct	its	provision	of	legal	services.	Centro	Legal	instead	alleges	
that,	if	independent	 adjudicators	 reactivate	 certain	 proceedings,	Centro	 Legal
will	have	to	perform	additional	legal	work	for	existing	clients.	Appl.	22–24.	Characterizing	that	contingent	workload	as	“unfunded”	does	not	transform	increased	
demand	for	the	organization’s	ordinary	services	into	the	direct	operational	interference	recognized	in Havens.	Moreover,	four	months	after	judgment,	Centro	
Legal	still	identifies	no	case	re-calendared	because	of	the	Consent	Judgment,	no	
imminent	hearing	or	deadline,	and	no	expenditure	actually	incurred.
Applicants’	attacks	on	the	Consent	Judgment	do	not	improve	their	position.	The	Rule	remained	binding	when	Texas	sued;	the	Executive’s	policy	memorandum	 did	 not	 vacate	 it	 or	 redress	 Texas’s	 alleged	 injuries.	 A	 federal

5
defendant’s	 agreement	 that	 a	 rule	 is	 unlawful	 does	 not	 erase	 a	 controversy	
where	the	rule	remains	operative	and	judicial	relief	changes	the	parties’	legal	
relationship.	Nor	is	judicial	vacatur	under	5	U.S.C.	§ 706	an	agency	repeal	governed	by	§ 553.	Applicants’	statutory	arguments	concern	a	materially	broader	
2024	Rule	that	no	court	of	appeals	has	reviewed,	and	the	authorities	they	invoke	 construed	 earlier	 regulations.	 Their	 remedial	 objections,	 even	 if	 ultimately	substantial,	cannot	justify	reinstating	the	entire	Rule	at	the	request	of	
nonparties	who	identify	no	injury	from	its	unrelated	provisions.
Finally,	Applicants	show	no	likely	irreparable	harm.	Their	application	recycles	the	same	August	declarations	rejected	below	and	supplies	no	evidence	
of	any	concrete	harm	during	the	intervening	months.	By	contrast,	a	stay	would	
revive	a	rule	the	district	court	declared	unlawful,	renew	the	fiscal	and	sovereign	
injuries	Texas	alleged,	and	unsettle	a	final	judgment	accepted	by	the	actual	parties.	 It	would	also	 restore	a	 binding	 regulation	 that	 the	 Federal	Government	
would	have	to	administer	unless	and	until	lawfully	displaced,	even	though	responsible	officials	concluded	 that	 the	Rule	cannot	be	defended	in	good	 faith.	
The	application	should	be	denied.

6
STATEMENT
I. The	Rule	and	the	Consent	Judgment
In	May	2024,	 the	Department	of	 Justice	promulgated	Efficient	Case	and	
Docket	Management	in	Immigration	Proceedings,	89	Fed.	Reg.	46,742	(May	29,	
2024)	(the	“Rule” or	“Administrative	Closure	Rule”).	Among	other	changes,	the	
Rule	authorized	immigration	judges	and	the	Board	of	Immigration	Appeals	to	
administratively	 close	 removal	 proceedings	 under	 a	 totality-of-the-circumstances	 standard,	 including	 when	 no	 collateral	 petition,	 application,	 or	 proceeding	was	pending.	Id. at	46,792;	App.	86a–87a.	Texas	contends	that	the	Rule	
transformed	administrative	closure	from	a	limited	docket-management	device	
into	indefinite	non-adjudication,	even	though	the	Immigration	and	Nationality	
Act	directs	that,	“[a]t	the	conclusion	of	the	proceeding,”	the	immigration	judge	
“shall	decide	whether	an	alien	is	 removable.”	8	U.S.C.	§ 1229a(c)(1)(A);	App.	
1a–43a.
In	April	2025,	Acting	Director	of	the	Executive Office for Immigration 
Review (“EOIR”) issued	Policy	Memorandum	25-29. The	memorandum	states
that	no	statute	authorizes	administrative	closure,	criticized	the	Rule’s	legal	and	
factual	premises,	and	announced	that	EOIR	could	not	defend	the	Rule	in	good	
faith.	 App.	 100a–108a.	 But	 the	 memorandum	 did	 not	 rescind,	 vacate,	 or

7
suspend	 the	Rule.	The	Rule	“remain[ed]	in	 full	legal	 force	and	continue[d]	 to	
bind	EOIR	adjudicators.”	App.	87a (alteration	in	original).
Texas	filed	this	action	on	June	22,	2026,	alleging	that	the	Rule	exceeded	
EOIR’s	statutory	authority,	violated	the	Administrative	Procedure	Act,	and	imposed	continuing	fiscal,	public-safety,	and	sovereign	harms	on	Texas.	App.	1a–
43a.	Texas’s	complaint	challenged	the	Administrative	Closure	Rule	and	asked	
the	district	court	to	“vacate,	set	aside,	and	permanently	enjoin	Defendants	from	
implementing	it,”	to	declare	that	the	Rule	exceeded	statutory	authority,	and	to	
declare	that	no	statute	authorizes	immigration judges	to	administratively	close	
or	suspend	adjudication	of	a	case.	App.	42a.
Texas	 and	 the	 federal	 defendants	jointly	moved	 for	 entry	 of	 a	 consent	
judgment.	App.	44a–48a.	The	parties	agreed	that	the	Rule	authorized	indefinite	
closure	without	legal	justification	or	identifiable	timetables and	that	the	Rule	
was	inadequately	justified	and	arbitrary	and	capricious.	App.	44a–46a.	The	district	court	entered	an	Order	and	Final	Judgment	(the	“Consent	Judgment”)	after	
considering	the	complaint,	the	joint	motion,	and	applicable	law.	App.	49a–50a.	
The	judgment	declares the	Rule	contrary	to	law	and	in	excess	of	statutory	authority;	declares that	no	statute	authorizes	immigration	judges	to	indefinitely	
administratively	close	or	suspend	adjudication	of	a	case;	permanently	enjoins
enforcement	of	the	Rule;	enjoins regulations	permitting	such	closure	without

8
reaching	 the	merits	absent	an	express	 statutory	 basis;	 vacates the	Rule;	and	
records the	parties’	waiver	of	appeal.	Id.
II. Applicants’	 Unsuccessful	 Requests	 for	 Intervention	 and	 Emergency	Relief
On	August	7,	2026,	the	Cities	of	Baltimore,	Columbus,	and	New	Haven	and	
Centro	Legal	de	la	Raza	moved	to	intervene	as	defendants	under	Federal	Rule	
of	Civil	Procedure	24(a)(2)	for	the	purpose	of	appealing	the	Consent	Judgment.	
App.	86a–87a.	Because	the	existing	parties	would	not	appeal,	Applicants	had	to	
demonstrate	 their	 own	Article	 III	 standing	 to	 pursue	 that	 relief.	 See	Virginia	
House,	587	U.S.	at	663–64.
The	district	court	denied	intervention.	App.	88a–94a.	Applying	Fifth	Circuit	precedent	requiring	a	futility	inquiry	when	proposed	defense	intervenors	
seek	to	assert	defenses	no	existing	party	advances,	the	court	held	that	none	of	
the	Applicants	had	Article	III	standing	to	prosecute	the	contemplated	appeal.	
App.	 88a–94a	 (citing	United	 States	 v.	 Texas,	 181	 F.4th	 548,	 553–54	 (5th	 Cir.	
2026)).
The	court	rejected	the	Cities’	predicted	loss	of	municipal	income-tax	revenue	because	it	depended	on	“recalendaring;	an	adverse	merits	decision;	a	final	
removal	 order;	 execution	 of	 that	 order;	 the	individual’s	 continued	 residence	
and	taxable	employment	in	the	same	city	absent	removal;	and	a	resulting	net

9
revenue	loss.”	App.	90a.	The	direct	consequence	of	 the	Consent	 Judgment,	at	
most,	is	that	some	cases	may	be	recalendared;	ultimate	removal	turns	on	separate	adjudicatory	and	enforcement	decisions.	App.	91a.	The	court	also	held	Baltimore’s	 voluntary	 expenditures	 on	 immigration	 legal	 services	to	 be	 self-inflicted	 and	 rejected	 the	 Cities’	 U-visa	 theory	 as	 dependent	 on	 speculative	
choices	by	unidentified	victims,	witnesses,	adjudicators,	prosecutors,	and	enforcement	officials.	App.	91a–92a.
The	district	court	separately	held	that	Centro	Legal’s	increased-workload	
theory	 was	 “explicitly	 foreclosed”	 by	 the	 en	 banc	 Fifth	 Circuit’s	 decision	 in	
United	States	v.	Texas,	173	F.4th	659,	666	(5th	Cir.	2026).	App.	93a.	Centro	Legal’s	 prediction	 that	 it	 might	 perform	 more	 work	 for	 current	 clients,	 accept	
fewer	new	matters,	or	experience	reputational	effects	was	the	same	derivative	
organizational	injury	that	binding	precedent	rejected.	App.	93a–94a.
The	district	court	did	not	address	the	other	requirements	 for	intervention	under	Rule	24(a)(2).
Applicants	noticed	an	appeal	and	sought	a	stay	in	the	district	court.	The	
court	denied	that	motion,	explaining	that	Applicants	could	not	appeal	or	obtain	
a	stay	of	the	underlying	judgment	because	they	had	been	denied	intervention	
and	remained	nonparties.	App.	95a.	It	further	held	that	they	failed	to	satisfy	the	
traditional	stay	factors.	Id.

10
Applicants	then	asked	the	Fifth	Circuit	to	stay	the	Consent	Judgment	and	
summarily	 reverse	 the	intervention	 denial.	 The	 Fifth	 Circuit	 denied	 both	 requests.	 App.	 98a–99a.	Applicants’ appeal	 from	 the	denial	 of	intervention	 remains	pending.
STANDARD
An	applicant	seeking	a	stay	from	this	Court	must	establish	“(1)	a	reasonable	probability	that	four	Justices	will	consider	the	issue	sufficiently	meritorious	to	grant	certiorari;	(2)	a	fair	prospect	that	a	majority	of	the	Court	will	vote	
to	reverse	the	judgment	below;	and	(3)	a	likelihood	that	irreparable	harm	will	
result	from	the	denial	of	a	stay.”	Hollingsworth	v.	Perry,	558	U.S.	183,	190	(2010)	
(per	curiam).	The	Court	also	considers	the	harms	to	the	opposing	parties	and	
the	public	interest.	Ohio	v.	EPA,	603	U.S.	279,	291	(2024).	A	stay	“is	not	a	matter	
of	right,”	and	the	applicant	bears	the	burden	of	showing	that	the	circumstances	
justify	this	Court’s	intervention.	Nken	v.	Holder,	556	U.S.	418,	433–34	(2009).
Applicants	cannot	satisfy	that	standard.
REASONS	FOR	DENYING	THE	APPLICATION

11
I. Applicants Have Not Demonstrated a Reasonable Probability That 
This Court Will Grant Certiorari.
Applicants	must	show	a	reasonable	probability	that	this	Court	will	grant	
certiorari,	 not	 merely	 that	 they	 disagree	 with	 the	 Consent	 Judgment.	 Hollingsworth,	558	U.S.	at	190.	They	have	not	made	that	showing.	The	Fifth	Circuit	
has	yet	to	decide	whether	Applicants	may	intervene,	much less	addressed	their	
challenges	to	the	underlying	judgment.	Indeed,	even	if	Applicants	were	to	prevail	before	the	Fifth	Circuit,	the	most	likely	result	would	be	a	remand	 for	the	
district	 court	 to	 consider	 the	 other	 intervention	 requirements	 under	 Rule	
24(a)(2).	Applicants	 identify	 no	 conflict	 on	 the	 standing	 questions	 this	 case	
presently	raises,	and	the	prior	Arizona	proceedings—which	involved	different	
issues—do	 not	 establish	 that	 review	is	warranted	 here.	Whatever	 questions	
might	 eventually	 merit	 this	 Court’s	 consideration,	 the	 intervention	 appeal	
should	first	run	its	course.	Applicants	offer	no	sufficient	reason	to	depart	from	
that	ordinary	sequence	or	to	expect	this	Court	to	do	so.
A. There	is	no	court	of	appeals	judgment	on	the	intervention	appeal,	
much less	on	the	merits.
The	 Fifth	 Circuit	 has	 not	 adjudicated	 Applicants’	 appeal of	 the	 district	
court’s	denial	of	the	motion	to	intervene	for	lack	of	standing.	Its	two-page	order	
denied	interim	relief	and	summary	reversal	without	deciding	the	appeal.	App.	
98a–99a.	 It	 has	 never	 addressed	 Applicants’	 challenges	 to	 the	 Consent

12
Judgment.	Indeed,	because	Applicants	remain	nonparties,	those	merits	issues	
are	not	presently	within	the	permissible	scope	of	their	appeal.	See Nuclear	Regulatory	Commission v.	Texas,	605	U.S.	665,	 679–80 (2025).
Applicants cannot,	 at	 this	 stage,	identify	 any	 court	 of	 appeals	 decision	
that	creates	a	conflict,	resolves	an	important	question	incorrectly,	or	otherwise	
warrants	certiorari.	
Rule	11	reflects	the	Court’s	settled	reluctance	to	intervene	before	judgment.	Certiorari	before	judgment	is	available	only	when	a	case	is	“of	such	imperative	public	importance	as	to	justify	deviation	from	normal	appellate	practice	and	to	require	immediate	determination	in	this	Court.”	Applicants	neither	
invoke	Rule	11	nor	make	that	showing.	Their	intervention	appeal	can	proceed	
in	the	ordinary	course.	
The	absence	of	a	reasoned	appellate	decision	is	especially	consequential	
because	 the	district	court	resolved	only	 threshold	standing;	it	did	not	decide	
the	remaining	Rule	24	requirements.	App.	89a-94a.	Even	if	the	Fifth	Circuit	disagreed	on	standing,	the	ordinary	remedy	would	be	a	remand	 for	those	unresolved	issues regarding	the	remaining	Rule	24	requirements.	The	Fifth	Circuit	
would	be	highly	unlikely	 to	address	 those	requirements	in	 the	 first	instance,	
much	less	review	challenges	to	the	underlying	judgment that	had	not	yet	been	
presented	to	the	district	court.

13
Applicants’	assertion	 that	administrative	closure	is	important	does	not	
cure	 the	vehicle	problem.	 Importance	alone	does	not	 transform	a	 fact-bound	
standing,	splitless dispute	into	a	suitable	case	 for	certiorari	before	judgment.	
And	the	lack	of	any	analysis	by	any	court	regarding	Applicants’	challenges	to	
the	Rule’s	statutory	validity	is	a	reason	to	wait for	the	lower	courts,	not	a	reason	
for	this	Court	to	decide	the	issue	first.	This	Court	is	“a	court	of	review,	not	of	
first	view.”	Cutter	v.	Wilkinson,	544	U.S.	709,	718	n.7	(2005).
A. The	prior	Arizona	proceedings	do	not	establish	a	probability	of	
review	here.
Applicants	have	 failed	 to	show	a	reasonable	probability	that	 this	Court	
will	grant	certiorari.	In	making	their	argument,	Applicants	rely	heavily	on	Arizona	v.	City	&	County	 of	San	Francisco and	Arizona	v.	Mayorkas.	Appl.	12–17.	
Neither	supplies	the	missing	probability	of	certiorari.
In	City	&	County	of	San	Francisco,	the	Court	granted	certiorari	after	the	
Ninth	Circuit	had	ruled	on	intervention.	596	U.S.	at	763.	This Court	 then	dismissed	the	writ	as	improvidently	granted.	Id. The	four-Justice	concurrence	on	
which	Applicants	rely	did	not	decide	that	intervention	was	required	or	that	litigation	acquiescence	violated	the	APA.	It	catalogued	numerous	unresolved	issues—standing,	mootness,	vacatur,	the	scope	of	relief,	and	the	interaction	between	 judicial	 judgments	 and	 rulemaking—and	 concluded	 that	 this	 “mare’s

14

III. Applicants’ Challenges to the Consent Judgment Do Not Establish a 
Fair Prospect of Reversal and Are Not Properly Before the Court Unless Intervention Is Granted.
The	district	court	properly	exercised	its	authority	under	the	APA	to	resolve	Texas’s	challenge	to	a	binding	federal	rule	and	set	aside	agency	action	that	
exceeded	statutory	limits.	The	federal	defendants’	agreement	with	Texas’s	legal	
position	did	not,	by	itself,	deprive	the	district	court	of	authority	to	resolve	the	
controversy. Applicants	 devote	much	 of	 their	 application	 to the	 validity	 and	
scope	of	the	Consent	Judgment.	Appl.	26–33.

27
Those	arguments	are	premature	because	Applicants	cannot	appeal	that	
judgment	unless	they	first	become	parties.	Virginia	House,	587	U.S.	at	663–64.
Even	if	these	arguments	were	properly	before	this	Court,	they	fail	to	establish	
a	fair	prospect	of	reversal.
A. The	case	presented	a	 live	controversy	even	 though	 the	defendants	agreed	with	Texas’s	legal	position.
Texas’s	 challenge	 presented	 a	 live	 controversy	 because	 the	 Rule	 remained	 binding	 and	 continued	 to	 cause	injuries	 that	 the	 federal	 defendants’	
agreement	with	Texas	did	nothing	to	remedy.	App.	19a–28a,	107a.	Applicants	
characterize	the	action	as	a	“friendly	sui[t]”	because	Texas	and	the	federal	defendants	agreed	that	the	Rule	was	unlawful	and	jointly	sought	judgment.	Appl.	
6.	Agreement	over	liability	or	remedy	does	not	itself	eliminate	Article	III	jurisdiction	where	the	challenged	legal	regime	remains	operative	and	judicial	relief	
alters	the	parties’	legal	relationship.
When	Texas	sued,	the	Rule	remained	binding	on	EOIR	adjudicators.	App.	
87a,	100a–108a.	EOIR’s	Policy	Memorandum	25-29,	App100a-108a, criticized	
the	Rule	and	announced	a	litigation	position,	but	it	did	not	vacate,	repeal,	suspend,	or	cease	enforcement	of	the	regulation.	Texas	plausibly	alleged	that	the	
operative	Rule	caused	continuing	fiscal	and	sovereign	injuries.	App.	19a–28a.

28
Only	a	judicial	judgment	could	provide	the	vacatur,	declaration,	and	binding	injunctive	relief	Texas	sought.	App.	42a,	49a–50a.
This	Court	has	repeatedly	recognized	that	the	government’s	agreement	
with	a	claimant’s	legal	position	does	not	necessarily	eliminate	a	case	or	controversy	when	the	challenged	law	remains	operative	and	the	judgment	has	concrete	 legal	 consequences.	 See	 INS	 v.	 Chadha,	 462	 U.S.	 919,	 939–40	 (1983);	
United	States	v.	Windsor,	570	U.S.	744,	755–63	(2013).	Consent	judgments	are	
a	routine	means	of	resolving	genuine	disputes,	provided	they	“spring	from	and	
serve	 to	resolve	a	dispute	within	 the	court’s	subject-matter	jurisdiction”	and	
remain	within	the	general	scope	of	the	pleadings.	Local	No.	93,	Int’l	Ass’n of	Firefighters	v.	City	of	Cleveland,	478	U.S.	501,	525–26	(1986).	The	district	court	expressly	found	jurisdiction	and	entered	relief	addressing	claims	and	a	prayer	for	
relief	pleaded	by	Texas.	App.	42a,	44a–50a.
Applicants’	historical	authorities	involved	manufactured	proceedings	in	
which	 no	 genuine	legal	injury	 or	 adverse	legal	 relationship	 existed.	 See,	 e.g.,	
United	 States	 v.	Johnson,	 319	 U.S.	 302,	 304–05	 (1943).	 That	 is	 not	 this	 case.	
Texas	is	a	separate	sovereign	alleging	concrete	injuries	from	a	binding	federal	
rule.	 The	 Federal	 Government’s	 decision	 to	 acknowledge	 legal	 error	neither	
manufactured those	injuries	nor	erased the	Rule’s	legal	effect.

29
Applicants	identify	no	 false	 fact or sham	plaintiff	suggesting	that	Texas	
lacked	the	injuries	it	alleged.	At	most,	they	dispute	whether	the	district	court’s	
legal	 conclusions	 and	 remedy	 were	 correct—questions	 that	 could	 be	 raised
through	ordinary	appellate	review if	they	were	permitted	to	intervene.
B. Section	553	governs	agency	rulemaking,	not	a	court’s	exercise	of	
judicial	review	under	Section	706.
A	court	may	set	aside	an	unlawful	rule	under	§	706	without	conducting	
the	 notice-and-comment	 proceedings	 that	 §	 553	 requires	 of	 agencies.	Applicants’	APA	argument	conflates	agency	repeal	with	judicial	relief.	Section	553	
prescribes	procedures	an	agency	generally	must	 follow	when	it	promulgates,	
amends,	or	repeals	a	legislative	rule.	Perez	v.	Mortg. Bankers	Ass’n,	575	U.S.	92,	
101	(2015).	The	federal	defendants	did	not	issue	a	repeal	here.	Texas	invoked	
judicial	 review,	and	 the	district	court	entered	a	judgment	declaring	 the	Rule	
unlawful	and	setting	it	aside	under	5	U.S.C.	§	706(2).	App.	44a–50a.
Nothing	in	§	553	makes	notice	and	comment	a	prerequisite	to	a	federal	
court’s	exercise	of	judicial	review.	Sections	551(5)	and	553	govern	an	agency’s	
formulation,	 amendment,	 or	 repeal	 of	 a	 rule.	 Section	 706	 assigns	 a	 different	
function	to	the	reviewing	court:	it	must	“decide	all	relevant	questions	of	law”	
and	“hold	unlawful	and	set	aside”	agency	action	that	exceeds	statutory	authority	or	is	otherwise	not	in	accordance	with	law.	5	U.S.C.	§	706;	see Loper	Bright

30
Enterprises	v.	Raimondo,	603	U.S.	369,	391–92	 (2024)	 (explaining	 that	 §	706	
requires	courts	to	exercise	independent	judgment	in	determining	whether	an	
agency	acted	within	its	statutory	authority); FCC	v.	NextWave	Pers. Commc’ns
Inc.,	537	U.S.	293,	300	(2003)	(“The	Administrative	Procedure	Act	requires	federal	 courts	 to	 set	aside	 federal	agency	action	 that	is	 ‘not	in	accordance	with	
law.’” (quoting	5	U.S.C.	§	706(2)(A))).	A	court	performing	that	statutory	duty	
exercises	judicial-review	authority;	it	does	not	itself	formulate,	amend,	or	repeal	a	rule	under	§	553.	Whether	the	district	court	correctly	determined	that	
this	Rule	was	unlawful	and	properly	scoped	the	resulting	relief	presents	separate	merits	and	remedial	questions,	but	neither	question	transforms	the	court’s	
judgment	into	agency	rulemaking	subject	to	notice	and	comment.
Consumer	 Energy	 Council	 of	 America	 v.	 FERC,	 673	 F.2d	 425	 (D.C.	 Cir.	
1982),	does	not	establish	otherwise.	There,	the	agency	itself	attempted	to	revoke	a	rule	without	notice	and	comment	and	argued	that	it	was	merely	correcting	a	defect.	Id. at	446–48.	The	case	did	not	hold	that	a	court	may	never	set	aside	
an	 unlawful	 rule	 when	 the	 agency	 confesses	 error.	 Likewise,	 Conservation	
Northwest	v.	Sherman,	715	F.3d	1181	(9th	Cir.	2013),	and	United	States	v.	Carpenter,	526	F.3d	1237	(9th	Cir.	2008),	concerned	settlements	that	themselves	
imposed	or	amended	substantive	regulatory	obligations	contrary	to	governing	
law.	The	Consent	Judgment	here	does	not	promulgate	a	replacement	regulation.

31
It	adjudicates	the	legality	of	existing	agency	action	and	grants	the	relief	Texas	
pleaded.
Applicants	rely	on	 the	 four-Justice	concurrence	in	City	&	County	of	San	
Francisco.	But	this Court	dismissed	that	case	as	improvidently	granted. 596	U.S.	
at	763,	765–66.	The	circumstances	there	were	also	distinct:	after	lower	courts	
had	adjudicated	the	public-charge	rule	and	the	government	dismissed	appeals,	
DHS	relied	on	a	judgment	from	separate	litigation	to then remove	the	rule	from	
the	 Code	 of	 Federal	 Regulations	without	 notice	 and	 comment.	Id. at	 764–65	
(Roberts,	C.J.,	concurring).	Here,	the	challenged	act	is	the	judgment	itself,	entered	in	Texas’s	direct	APA	action.	Whether	that	judgment	was	correct	is	a	judicial-review	question—not	an	agency	repeal	subject	to	§	553.
The	prospective	injunction	does	not	require	the	Federal	Government	to	
violate	the	APA.	It	prohibits	substantially	similar	regulations	authorizing	broad	
administrative	closure	“absent	an	express	statutory	basis.”	App.	50a.	It	neither	
requires	promulgation	of	a	new	rule	nor	specifies	the	content	of	any	replacement	 regulation.	 If	later	legal	 developments	justify	modification,	 the	 Federal	
Rules	provide	mechanisms	to	seek	it.	The	injunction’s	breadth	may	be	litigated	
by	 a	 proper	 party,	 but	it	 does	 not	 transform	the	 judgment	into	 an	 unlawful	
agency	repeal.

32
C. Applicants	have	not	shown	that	the	2024	Rule	is	clearly	authorized	by	the	INA.
The	Attorney	General’s	authority	 to	manage	immigration	dockets	must	
operate	within	the	framework	Congress	prescribed	for	deciding	removability.	
Applicants’	statutory	argument	is,	at	minimum,	substantially	disputed.	The	Attorney	General’s	general	authority	to	supervise	EOIR	and	“establish	such	regulations”	as	necessary,	8	U.S.C.	§ 1103(g)(2),	does	not	permit	rules	inconsistent	
with	Congress’s	specific	removal-adjudication	framework.	Section	1229a	provides	 that	 proceedings	 under	 that	 section	are	 the	 “sole	and	exclusive	 procedure”	for	determining	removability	and	directs	that,	“[a]t	the	conclusion	of	the	
proceeding,”	the	immigration	judge	“shall	decide	whether	an	alien	is	removable.”	8	U.S.C.	§	1229a(a)(3),	(c)(1)(A).
Texas	alleges that	the	2024	Rule	did	not	merely	permit	short,	case-specific	pauses	tied	to	a	pending	collateral	matter but	that	it	authorized	administrative	closure	based	on	a	broad	totality-of-the-circumstances	test	even	when	
no	collateral	petition,	application,	or	action	was	pending,	and	it	permitted	closure	without	an	identifiable	 timetable	 for	 resolution.	89	Fed.	Reg.	at	46,792;
App.	1a–43a.	According	to	the	complaint	and	the	joint	motion,	administrative	
closure	 had	 often	lasted	 years	 or	 decades	and	left	 hundreds	 of	 thousands	 of	
proceedings	without	adjudication.	App.	3a–4a,	45a–46a.	A	general	procedural

33
delegation	does	not	obviously	authorize	a	mechanism	that	operates	in	practice	
as	indefinite	non-adjudication	of	matters	Congress	directed	immigration	judges	
to	decide.
Administrative	closure	is	not	equivalent	 to	an	 ordinary	continuance.	A	
continuance	ordinarily	keeps	a	matter	on	the	active	docket	and	postpones	it	to	
a	future	date	or	identifiable	event.	The	Rule	permitted	removal	from	the	active	
docket	without	a	fixed	return	date	or	pending	collateral	matter.	Applicants’	observation	that	a	party	could	later	seek	recalendaring	does	not	answer	whether	
the	Attorney	General	may	authorize	indefinite	suspension	in	the	first	place.
The	appellate	cases	Applicants	invoke	do	not	establish	 the	2024	Rule’s	
legality.	Romero,	Meza	Morales,	and	Arcos	Sanchez construed	whether	earlier	
regulations	implicitly	authorized	administrative	closure.	They	did	not	decide	
whether	the	2024	Rule’s	express	and	expanded	regime	is	consistent	with	the	
INA.	The	Sixth	Circuit,	considering	the	same	earlier	regulatory	framework,	concluded	 that	administrative	 closure	 did	 not	 constitute	a	 “disposition”	and	 observed	that	permanent	closure	of	hundreds	of	thousands	of	cases	was	largely	
contrary	 to	law.	Hernandez-Serrano,	 981	 F.3d	at	 463–66.	Hernandez-Serrano
does	not	resolve	this	case,	but	its	reasoning	supports	Texas’s	position	that	general	docket-management	authority	does	not	permit	indefinite	suspension	of	removal	proceedings.

34
Applicants’	 reliance	 on	longstanding	 practice	likewise	 does	 not	 supply	
statutory	 authority.	 Administrative	 agencies	 cannot	 acquire	 power	 through	
repetition.	There	is	“no	authority	for	the	doctrine	that	the	Executive	can	acquire	
authority	 forbidden	 by	 law	 through	 a	 process	 akin	 to	 adverse	 possession.”	
Biden	v.	Texas,	597	U.S.	785,	830	(2022)	(Alito,	 J.,	dissenting).	The	Homeland	
Security	Act	preserved	statutory	“authorities	and	functions”	exercised	by	EOIR,	
8	U.S.C.	§	1103(g)(1);	it	did	not	silently	ratify	every	informal	docket	practice	or	
eliminate	limits	imposed	by	the	INA.	And	the	existence	of	specific	regulations	
or	settlements	authorizing	closure	in	defined	circumstances	cuts	against	inferring	unlimited	general	authority.
Applicants	have	not	shown	 that	 the	Attorney	General’s	general	 regulatory	authority	permits	indefinite	suspension	of	proceedings	Congress	directed	
immigration	judges	to	decide.	See	8	U.S.C.	§	1229a(a)(3),	(c)(1)(A).		Their	statutory	 arguments	 therefore	 fail	 to	 establish	 a	 fair	 prospect	 of	 reversal,	 even	
apart	from	their	failure	to	establish	standing	or	a	right	to	intervene.
D. Applicants’	remedial	objections	cannot	justify	staying	the	entire	
judgment.
Any	stay	must	be	tailored	to	Applicants’	own	likely	injuries,	and	their	objections	to	discrete	portions	of	the	Consent	Judgment	do	not	justify	suspending	
it	in	 full.	Applicants	argue	 that	 the	judgment	should	have	severed	provisions

35
unrelated	to	administrative	closure	and	should	not	have	included	prospective	
relief.	Appl.	31–33.	Those	objections	do	not	support	the	stay	they	request for	
four	reasons.
First,	Texas’s	complaint	challenged	the	Administrative	Closure	Rule	and	
requested	that	it	be	vacated,	set	aside,	and	permanently	enjoined.	App.	42a.	The	
joint	 motion	 likewise	 stated	 that	 Texas	 challenged	 the	 Rule’s	 regulatory	
changes,	including	the	rescission	of	the	2020	rule,	and	requested	vacatur	of	the	
Rule.	 App.	 44a–46a.	 Applicants	 may	 dispute	 whether	 every	 provision	 was	
properly	 included,	 but	 the	 judgment	 did	 not	 grant	 relief	 wholly	 outside	 the	
pleadings.
Second,	Applicants	lack	standing	to	challenge	portions	of	the	Rule	unrelated	to	any	asserted	injury.	Their	claimed	harms	concern	administrative	closure,	 termination	of	certain	cases,	and	downstream	consequences	 for	clients	
and	municipalities.	They	identify	no	injury	from	briefing	schedules,	background	
checks,	or	sua	sponte	reopening	rules.	An	alleged	severability	error	affecting	
provisions	that	do	not	injure	Applicants	cannot	support	their	intervention	or	
this	stay.
Third,	even	if	a	reviewing	court	ultimately	narrowed	the	prospective	injunction	or	restored	a	severable	ancillary	provision,	that	would	not	justify	suspending	the	entire	judgment	and	reinstating	the	administrative-closure	regime

36
now.	Equitable	relief	must	be	tailored	to	the	applicant’s	likely	injury.	Applicants	
propose	no	narrower	stay	tied	to	a	concrete	harm.	Their	all-or-nothing	request

Fourth,	the	injunction	is	narrower	than	Applicants	portray	it.	It	does	not	
forever	prohibit	every	form	of	administrative	closure.	It	bars	regulations	permitting	 immigration	 judges	 to	 administratively	 close	 proceedings	 without	
reaching	the	merits	“absent	an	express	statutory	basis	to	do	so.”	App.	50a.	Applicants	identify	no	pending	rulemaking	or	imminent	agency	proposal	impaired	
by	that	provision.	Any	challenge	to	hypothetical	future	effects	is	not	a	basis	for	
emergency	reinstatement	of	the	existing	Rule.
IV. Applicants Have Not Demonstrated Likely Irreparable Harm.
The	Consent	Judgment	should	remain	in	effect	because	Applicants	have	
not	shown	that	it	is	likely	to	cause	them	irreparable	harm	during	the	appeal.	
See	Nken,	556	U.S.	at	434–35.	Applicants’	irreparable-harm	claims largely	repeat	the	injuries	the	district	court	held	too	speculative	for	standing.	An	injury	
that	is	conjectural	and	causally	attenuated	does	not	become	likely	and	imminent	merely	because	it	is	relabeled	“irreparable.”	See id.
The	Cities	identify	no	taxpayer	likely	to	be	removed	during	the	appeal,	no	
amount	 of	 revenue	 likely	 to	 be	 lost,	 and	 no	 evidence	 that	 the	 judgment	 has

37
reduced	municipal	receipts.	Their	reliance	on	Alabama	Association	of	Realtors	
v.	Department	of	Health	and	Human	Services,	594	U.S.	758,	765	(2021) (per curiam),	is	misplaced.	The	landlords	there	were	subject	to	an	operative	moratorium	that	prevented	collection	of	rent	and	produced	actual,	unrecoverable	payment	losses.	Id.	Here,	no	legal	command	deprives	a	City	of	revenue;	any	loss	
depends	 on	 the	unresolved	chain	 of	adjudication,	enforcement,	employment,	
residence,	and	taxation	described	above.
The	Cities	likewise	identify	no	victim	who	has	declined	to	report	a	crime,	
no	witness	who	 has	 stopped	 cooperating,	 no	U-visa	applicant	 removed	midprosecution,	and	no	prosecution	that	has	failed.	Maryland	v.	King,	567	U.S.	1301,	
1303	(2012)	(Roberts,	C.J.,	in	chambers),	involved	a	sovereign’s	concrete	inability	to	enforce	a	duly	enacted	criminal	law.	It	does	not	establish	irreparable	
harm	whenever	a	municipality	predicts	that	third	parties	may	react	adversely	
to	a change	in	federal	procedure.
Centro	Legal	offers	projections,	not	imminent	facts.	Its	declaration	estimates	 the	hours	 that	might	be	required	if	matters	are	reactivated.	App.	63a–
70a.	It	does	not	identify	an	order	reopening	a	case,	an	upcoming	hearing,	a	new	
expert	expense,	an	employee hired,	a	grant	breached,	or	a	dollar	spent	because	
of	the	Consent	Judgment.	Applicants	filed	this	application	in	October,	months

38
after	the	June	22	judgment,	yet	provide	no	supplemental	declaration	showing	
that	any	predicted	harm	has	occurred	or	is	about	to	occur.

weeks	after	judgment	to	seek	intervention	and	more	than	two	months	to	seek

The	 public-interest	 examples	 concerning	 special	 immigrant	 juveniles	
(“SIJ”)	are	equally	contingent.	Appl.	34.	The	judgment	does	not	order	any	child	
removed,	require	recalendaring,	eliminate	SIJ	status,	or	prevent	case-specific

immigration	 cases,	 but	 generalized	 concern	 for	 unidentified	 persons	 cannot

V. The Equities and Public Interest Weigh Against a Stay.
The	balance	of	harms	and	the	public	interest	 favor	leaving	the	Consent	
Judgment	in	place	to	protect	Texas	from	renewed	injury	while	the	intervention	
appeal	proceeds	in	 the	ordinary	course.	A	stay	would	not	preserve	a	neutral	
status	quo.	It	would	revive	a	rule	that	has	been	vacated	since	June	22,	restore

39
authority	for	new	administrative	closures,	and	suspend	relief	obtained	by	the	
actual	parties.	It	would	also	restore	a	binding	regulation	that	the	Federal	Government	would	 have	 to	 administer	 unless	 and	 until	lawfully	 displaced,	 even	
though	 responsible	 officials	 concluded	 that	 the	 Rule	 cannot	 be	 defended	 in	
good	 faith.	 The	 Fifth	 Circuit	 has	 already	 declined	 to	 impose	 that	 disruption	
while	the	intervention	appeal	proceeds.	App.	98a–99a.
Texas	alleged	that	the	Rule	prolongs	the	presence	of	removable	aliens by	
indefinitely	 suspending	 adjudication	 and	 thereby	 increases	 state	 healthcare,	
education,	law-enforcement,	and	other	expenditures.	App.	19a–28a.	The	Consent	 Judgment	 redressed	 those	injuries	by	 vacating	 the	Rule	and	prohibiting	
substantially	similar	regulations	lacking	an	express	statutory	basis.	App.	49a–
50a.	A	stay	would	renew	the	same	alleged	harms	and	deprive	Texas	of	the	benefit	of	its	final	judgment.
The	harm	would	not	necessarily	end	when	the	stay	ends.	Cases	newly	administratively	closed	during	the	appeal	could	remain	dormant	for	years,	reproducing	 the	very	indefinite	delay	Texas	challenged.	The	parties	 to	 the	judgment	
have	accepted	its	finality	and	waived	appeal.	App.	50a.	Nonparties	should	not	unsettle	that	resolution	without	first	establishing	standing	and	a	right	to	intervene.
The	public	interest	favors	lawful	agency	action,	faithful	execution	of	Congress’s	 statutory	 scheme,	 finality	 of	 judgments,	 and	 orderly	 appellate

40
procedure.	 Applicants	 repeatedly	 invoke	 the	 fact	 that	 the	 Rule	 was	 promulgated	through	notice	and	comment.	Appl.	33–35.	Notice	and	comment	does	not	
immunize	an	agency	rule	from	judicial	review	or	authorize	it	to	exceed	the	statute.	The	district	court	entered	judgment	that	the	Rule	was	contrary	to	law.	App.	
49a–50a.	Restoring	that	Rule	before	Applicants	establish	party	status	would	invert	the	ordinary	sequence	of	review.
Applicants’	reliance	on	emergency	orders	staying	nationwide	relief	at	the	
request	of	the	Federal	Government	or	directly	regulated	parties	is	inapposite.	
See Appl.	34–35.	Those	applicants	possessed	party	status	and	asserted	direct	
sovereign	or	regulatory	injuries.	Here,	the	Federal	Government	does	not	seek	a	
stay,	Applicants	are	not	bound	or	regulated	by	the	judgment,	and	their	claimed	
harms	depend	on	multiple third	parties.	The	Court’s	equitable	power	does	not	
require	treating	those	distinct	postures	as	equivalent.
Nor	does	Mayorkas establish	that	the	equities	favor	Applicants.	The	stay	
there	expressly	left	the	Federal	Government	free	to	take	action	concerning	the	
policy,	and	the	Court	simultaneously	granted	certiorari	before	judgment	on	intervention.	143	S.	Ct.	at	478.	Applicants	request	a	stay	that	would	reinstate	a	
binding	regulation	while	seeking	no	immediate	merits	review	under	Rule	11.	
That	 would	 impose	 substantial	 present	 consequences	 without	 resolving	 the	
threshold	appeal.

41
Finally,	any	asserted	concern	about	“collusive	acquiescence,” Appl.	12-13,
remains	available	for	orderly	adjudication	if	a	litigant	with	standing	becomes	a

nonparty	must	first	establish	a	right	to	intervene	before	obtaining	substantive
